member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.AppearanceRepair
member.summary:
Makes a save that our own dec-cache bug already corrupted LOADABLE again.
stops us writing any more of them. This repairs the ones already on disk.
── WHAT IS WRONG WITH THOSE SAVES ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── A pawn was handed a HairStyleDec from a discarded parse generation, so the writer refused it and wrote "<name>_DELETED". On load, dec cannot resolve that name and — with no error, because a missing dec resolves to an empty string and then to null — hands the pawn a NULL HairStyle. The first time the map tries to draw that pawn, `RigController.UpdateAppearance` dereferences it, NREs, and `Map.Activate` never finishes: the map stays inactive forever and the log fills with thousands of "tried to update an inactive map".
── THE REPAIR ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Give the pawn a real hairstyle before the renderer touches it. `AppearanceData` is a CLASS, so the pawn keeps the repair: the next save writes a valid name and the save heals itself permanently.
★ This is deliberately a REPAIR, not a workaround: it does not paper over a live bug, because after DecCacheGuard no correctly-loaded pawn can reach here with a null hairstyle. If this ever fires on a save made AFTER the guard shipped, that is a real signal — so it says so, loudly, once.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.AshMat
member.summary: The .ashmat format: a mod's own material, as a handful of numbers and a few texture references.
member.remarks:
★★ WHY A FORMAT OF OUR OWN. The game's Material field is a path to a Godot .tres, and MeshRenderer applies it as a MaterialOverride — which beats anything baked into a .glb, so a mod's mesh wears whatever that path resolves to and nothing else. The bridge used to answer it with a flat colour, which made a material impossible to get wrong and equally impossible to get right. Reading a real .tres would mean a Godot text-resource parser inside the loader, resolving ext_resource paths of its own — a parser we do not have and do not want. A format we define is a few lines to read, and every texture reference in it goes back through the SAME resolver as everything else, so the sandbox, the .ashtex precedence and the placeholder rule apply for free.
★★ THIS FILE IS LINKED INTO THREE PROJECTS AND COMPILED, NEVER COPIED — the loader, the Godot shim that reads a material, and the gate that checks one before a mod may ship. They are three assemblies that cannot reference each other by design (the shim must share no type identity with the loader; the gate must not need a game), and a format whose key names are written down three times is a format whose halves drift. One file, three <Compile Include>s.
A reference is a full res:// path WITH its extension — res://mymod/crate_albedo.png — because that is exactly what the game would have asked for, so the resolver treats it identically and a pre-compressed .ashtex sibling still wins.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.AshTexFormat
member.summary: The .ashtex container: a texture already compressed for VRAM, optionally deflated for disk.
member.remarks:
★★ TWO DIFFERENT COMPRESSIONS, FOR TWO DIFFERENT COSTS, AND CONFUSING THEM IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THIS FILE. BC7 is what the GPU holds: it is fixed-rate, so it is the only way a mod texture reaches VRAM compressed at all, and the shipped game cannot produce it at runtime. Deflate is what the DISK holds: it costs nothing at rest and is undone once at load.
⚠ AND THE FIRST VERSION TRADED ONE FOR THE OTHER WITHOUT SAYING SO. A 256×256 icon measured 2,922 bytes as a .png and 87,424 as a raw .ashtex — **thirty times larger on disk** — because PNG is entropy-coded and BC7 is fixed-rate. The lane was described as bloat MITIGATION, which was true of VRAM and backwards for downloads. Deflating the payload measured 87,424 → 38,321 (56% off) on a real texture and 21,888 → 3,875 on a flat one, for the same bytes in VRAM.
v1 [magic ASBT][w][h][mips] raw BC7 16-byte header v2 [magic ASB2][w][h][mips][inflatedSize] deflated BC7 20-byte header
⚠ The v1 magic spells "TBSA" in a hex dump, not "ASBT" — it is written as a little-endian int32 and was chosen before anyone looked at the bytes. v2's is chosen so it reads "ASB2". Left alone rather than tidied: v1 files exist and one of them is the artifact every other proof is anchored to.
★★ THIS FILE IS LINKED INTO THE LOADER, THE GODOT SHIM AND THE GATE, never copied — the same rule as , for the same reason. Three assemblies that cannot reference each other must not each write a container format down separately. ⚠ The Mod Kit's writer is the one place that cannot link it (it ships to modders with no loader repo), so its test asserts these exact numbers.

member.summary: Installs the asset bridge: builds the resolver from the discovered mods and hands it to the small Godot-coupled assembly that subclasses ResourceFormatLoader.

★★ WHY THE WORK IS SPLIT ACROSS TWO BINARIES. This loader never compile-references GodotSharp — see : a HintPath here flows into four test projects and breaks the Linux loader build, and the loader compile-references neither dec nor the game assembly either. But a ResourceFormatLoader subclass cannot be produced by reflection: a Godot 4 C# type deriving from GodotObject needs the SDK's source generators to emit the glue that lets the ENGINE call a managed override, and without it the class compiles and is simply never called back into. The first smoke run logged only failures, so four of five assets read as healthy purely because nothing complained — and this project has been bitten by exactly that shape twice already: an animation path that had never run while its asset sat in a directory listing, and a pre-compressed texture silently demoted to a raw upload. member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.AssetBridgeResolver
member.summary: Every DECISION the asset bridge makes, with no Godot types anywhere in it.
member.remarks:
★ WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE, GODOT-FREE CLASS. The loader never compile-references GodotSharp — see for the reasoning (a HintPath here flows into four test projects and breaks the Linux loader build), and you cannot subclass ResourceFormatLoader by reflection. So the bridge is split: the Godot-coupled shim subclasses the engine type and holds NO policy, and everything that is actually a judgement — which mod owns a path, whether the path escapes its sandbox, which file on disk should serve it — lives here, where it can be tested without a game.
★★ ONE RESOLVER, USED BY BOTH _Exists AND _Load. This is the whole point and it is not stylistic. Two of the game's six asset converters branch on ResourceLoader.Exists before loading:
AudioStreamConverter "res://"+input+".wav" -> ".ogg" then s.ResourceName = input; // derefs PackedSceneConverter "res://"+input+".tscn" -> ".gltf" -> ".glb" returns it, with no null check
A loader that claims a rung it cannot serve makes them STOP on that rung: measured in-game, an ogg-only asset then threw a NullReferenceException from inside Ascent.Serialization — a stack trace blaming the game for a mod's missing file — and a glb-only scene returned null in silence. If existence and loading are ever computed from separate RULES they will disagree again.
★★ …BUT THEY ARE NOT THE SAME QUESTION. Both come from , and that has to stay true. What differs is what each does with a PLACEHOLDER: says no, because a stand-in is not an asset, and _Load hands it over, because by then the game is committed and the alternative is its own unguarded dereference. Answering "yes" to a probe was found to break a mod that was CORRECT — see for the ten call sites and what each of them meant to ask.
★★ ORDER HERE IS PRECEDENCE, NOT DISCOVERY. Because one method answers both "does anything serve this" and "WHICH file serves it", the rung it names must be the BEST one rather than the first one that happens to exist. Collapsing the two questions once already regressed this: the literal .png was tested first, so a pre-compressed .ashtex sibling lost, and every mod texture silently became a raw upload — BptcRgba 87,408 bytes to Rgba8 349,524 bytes. Runtime VRAM compression is categorically unavailable in the shipped game (measured every launch), so the .ashtex is the only route a mod texture has to reaching VRAM compressed at all.
★★ THE SANDBOX IS A SECURITY BOUNDARY, NOT TIDINESS. A dec asset path is author-controlled text that arrives at this class verbatim. Without 's containment check, "res://mod/../../.." would let any mod read any file the game process can read — through the component whose whole job is to be the trust anchor that verifies mod signatures. Rejections are attributed to the mod, loudly.

member.name: F:AshForge.ModLoader.AssetBridgeResolver.Placeholder
member.summary: Returned when the path is ours, nothing on disk serves it, and this is the LAST rung the game's converter will try — so the shim must hand back a visible stand-in rather than nothing.
member.remarks:
★★ ONLY EVER ON A FINAL RUNG, AND THAT IS THE ENTIRE SUBTLETY. A truthful _Exists is what makes the game's chained converters fall through: audio tries .wav then .ogg, scenes try .tscn then .gltf then .glb. Answering "yes, I have a placeholder" on an EARLY rung would strand the converter there and re-break the exact bug the shared resolver was written to fix — an ogg-only asset would never reach its .ogg. So a placeholder is offered only where the converter has nowhere left to go, and the early rungs still decline honestly.
★ Read out of the installed assembly, not a doc:
AudioStreamConverter "res://"+input+".wav" -> ".ogg", then audioStream.ResourceName = input; PackedSceneConverter "res://"+input+".tscn" -> ".gltf" -> ".glb" Texture2DConverter "res://"+input+".png" (one rung, so it is final) MeshConverter input+".glb" -> SceneUtility.GetMeshInstanceFrom(...)
The two that DEREFERENCE their result unchecked are audio and mesh, which is why a missing asset there arrives as a NullReferenceException from inside Ascent.Serialization — a stack trace blaming the game for a mod's missing file. .tres needs no entry here: it is synthesised unconditionally, so a material can never be missing in the first place.

member.name: M:AshForge.ModLoader.AssetBridgeResolver.Exists(System.String)
member.summary: Whether a REAL asset serves this path - a file on disk, or something we build in memory. A path we would only answer with a placeholder does NOT exist.
member.remarks:
★★ THIS IS WHAT _Exists MUST ASK, AND IT IS NOT THE SAME QUESTION AS . The bridge originally answered existence as "Resolve returned anything", which quietly included the placeholder sentinel - so for a mod-owned path the answer was always yes. That is right where the game uses Exists to walk a converter chain, which is the only use the design had looked at. It is wrong everywhere else, and the game has TEN other call sites:
GenderedResourceLoader "res://"+p+".glb" ELSE "pMale.glb"/"pFemale.glb" -> PICKS A PATH ApparelVariant if (Exists(MeshPath + "_Armor.glb")) -> OPTIONAL asset HairStyleDec if (Exists(...)) else FlatMesh = HideMesh -> OPTIONAL, has a fallback ApparelDec.VerifyVariants / WallDec.PostLoad(reporter) -> the GAME's OWN reporters
Answering yes at those turns a CORRECT mod into a broken one: a mod shipping fooMale.glb and fooFemale.glb - the convention the game itself defines - never reaches the gendered branch, because the probe for the plain foo.glb succeeded against a placeholder. It also silences the game's own missing-asset reports for exactly the audience they were written for.
★ THE SAFETY NET IS NOT LOST BY ANSWERING HONESTLY. Every one of the six converters calls ResourceLoader.Load UNCONDITIONALLY at the end of its chain, and the unguarded derefs in MeshRendererProps/StorageRendererProps/PlantRendererProps never probe at all - so a genuinely missing asset still reaches _Load and still gets its loud, attributed placeholder. Only the probe sites change, and every one of them changes toward what the game meant.
⚠ THE ONE THING THIS COSTS. GenderedResourceLoader returns (null, null) when no candidate exists and its callers dereference that, so a genuinely absent gendered asset is an NRE again rather than a placeholder. That case is caught before it can ship, by tools/AssetGate.

Registers the official ashforge.* capability catalog with the broker, each with its loader DEFAULT (the priority-0 floor). Called at startup BEFORE mod Init(), so a provider registered in a mod's Init finds its contract already defined.
★ HONEST DEVIATION from LOADER-BROKER-001 §11: the spec's defaults (e.g. "cheap sum of tracked items") assume the loader can read live game state, but the loader holds NO compile-time game reference (it reflects). So each loader default here is a NEUTRAL/EMPTY value, and richer standalone behavior comes from a mod registering its own provider — exactly the Raiders "keep your own calc as a priority-50 provider" pattern (WO-MIG-002), generalized. Flagged for the team: this is the right call given the no-game-ref constraint, but it means "net worth with zero mods" is 0, not an estimate.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.Contracts.BrokerContracts
member.summary:
Typed contract stubs for every published ashforge.* capability (broker spec §10.2).
WHY THIS EXISTS. Without it, a third-party author writes ctx.Query<ColonyNetWorth>(new CapabilityId( "ashforge", "colony.net_worth", 1)) — three facts (id, version, payload type) they have to get right from documentation, with a runtime type-guard rejection as the only feedback. Each stub below binds those three together in one place, so the compiler enforces what the broker would otherwise only reject at runtime. It is the difference between guessing at a channel and programming against a documented API.
★ THE STUBS DELIBERATELY DO NOT REDECLARE THE PAYLOAD TYPES. They reference the loader's ( et al). A copied payload type would be a DIFFERENT CLR Type in the mod's assembly, and the broker's runtime type guard compares against the contract's PayloadType — so every query would fall back to the default and every provider registration would be rejected. Same reason the Mod Kit ships these as a thin facade over AshLoader.dll, never as a standalone copy of the contracts.
★ Deriving a provider from ProviderBase makes BRK003 (declared version ≠ payload type) UNREPRESENTABLE: the capability id is supplied by the base, and the payload type is fixed by the generic. You choose only a priority (see the priority bands in HANDOFF_BROKER.md) and the pure read.
Every stub is a pure convenience wrapper — the underlying surface stays open for anyone who needs it. Adding a capability to without adding a stub here is caught by the "contract stub coverage" test in tools/BrokerTests.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.BrokerSaveDiagnostics
member.summary:
Save diagnostics (Resolution Panel spec §7, broker spec §9): remember WHICH PROVIDERS were bound to which capabilities when a save was written, and on load raise a non-blocking notice for any that changed.
"This save was created with Wealth & Trade providing colony net worth. It is now provided by Deep Economy Overhaul. Economy-derived values (raid scaling, prices) may differ."
INFORMATIONAL ONLY. It never gates loading — that would break save portability, which is the whole point of the standalone-first invariant. A save made with a provider installed must still load without it (resolving to the loader default), and vice versa.
★ WE RECORD BINDINGS, NOT VALUES. At load time nothing has been queried yet, so there is no provenance to compare against — but every provider has already registered (mod `Init` runs long before the sidecar is dispatched on `World.ActivateMap`). So the comparable, stable fact is "which provider WOULD win", computed the same way resolution computes it: effective priority desc, load order asc, skipping user-disabled and circuit-broken providers, falling through to the floor.
★ REGISTERED UNDER ITS OWN MOD ID, not . Fault counts are cumulative per id, and the core id is the capability default floor's id — pouring this diagnostic's faults into that bucket would muddy the floor's fault log (and, before the floor was made un-disableable, could have taken it down). This id is ordinary: if these callbacks ever throw repeatedly, the circuit breaker disables the diagnostics — which is exactly the right blast radius for a purely informational feature.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.Bus
member.summary:
The AshForge event bus — CORE (lives in the loader, not a mod), so it exists before anything subscribes. Mods publish and subscribe by name and never touch Harmony; AshForge owns the emit points (the Harmony postfixes that feed game events in) and the catalog of event names/payloads (see ).
THIN BY DESIGN (build sequence step 1): notification-only — fire-and-forget, order-irrelevant. No subscriber priority, no argument mutation, no cancellation yet; that "interception" layer is designed later against the first real interception consumer, not up front.
Isolation is not optional: a subscriber that throws is caught and attributed to its owning mod via , a mod auto-disabled by the fault policy stops receiving events, and one bad subscriber never breaks the publisher or its fellow subscribers.

The identity of a capability: a reserved-or-author namespace, a dotted name, and a schema MAJOR version. Canonical string form is namespace.name@version — e.g. ashforge.colony.net_worth@1.
Equality is case-insensitive on the JOINED name (see — the namespace/name split is not recoverable from the canonical string, so identity must not depend on it) and exact on version — net_worth@1 and net_worth@2 are DIFFERENT capabilities that coexist in the registry, which is how an old v1 consumer keeps working after a v2 ships (LOADER-BROKER-001 §4.1).
A single integer version is the schema major only: additive, backward-compatible changes do NOT bump it (a v1 consumer must tolerate extra fields); a schema-breaking change publishes a new contract at v2.

A first-party id is namespace ashforge + name colony.net_worth; a THIRD-PARTY id is namespace ashforge.mining + name production, since the loader itself requires third-party contracts to live under author.mod.*. member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.CapabilityOverrides
member.summary:
The user's provider overrides — reorder and disable — persisted in a LOADER config file, never inside a mod. (Resolution Panel spec §6.)
FILE: <ModsRoot>/ashloader.overrides.json.
★ SINGLE-WRITER BY CONSTRUCTION. The GAME is the only writer — the in-game panel is the one surface that mutates the store. The Hub READS this file (folding it into its manifest prediction, which is how the predicted view and the live view agree) and never writes it. That is not an accident to be fixed later: it is what lets two processes share the file with no lockfile, no merge, and no shutdown race. The only synchronization needed is that is ATOMIC, so a concurrent reader sees either the whole old file or the whole new one. Do not add a Hub write path without first adding a locking scheme.
Shape:
{ "format": 1, "capabilities": { "ashforge.colony.net_worth@1": [ { "providerModId": "ashforge.wealth", "effectivePriority": 150, "enabled": true } ] } }
INVARIANTS • **Mod-set tolerant.** An entry naming a provider that isn't installed is INERT, not an error — it simply never matches at registration. Reinstalling the mod re-activates the override. So we never prune entries for absent mods on save; that would silently destroy the user's intent whenever they disable a mod. • **Never breaks a consumer.** Disabling every provider still resolves: the loader default is not a provider, it's the floor (`InvokeDefault`). The worst a user override can do is degrade signal, never function. • **`effectivePriority` is nullable** — absent means "keep whatever the provider declared". Disabling a provider must not silently pin its priority. • Corrupt / unreadable file ⇒ NO overrides (log + carry on). An override store must never gate loading.

A crash, a full disk, or a concurrent reader (the Hub) can never observe a truncated or half-serialized store — the swap either happened or it didn't. A plain File.WriteAllText here would open the real file, truncate it, and only then start writing: a reader that lands in that window sees an EMPTY override set, i.e. every one of the user's choices silently reverted. Atomicity here is therefore only half the contract: every reader of this file must open it with FileShare.ReadWrite | FileShare.Delete (see , which the Hub mirrors), and the writer retries briefly to ride out a reader that is momentarily between opens.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.DecCacheGuard
member.summary:
Keeps the GAME's own static dec caches honest across the loader's repeated dec parses.
── THE BUG THIS EXISTS TO KILL (proven 2026-07-13) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── `Dec.Database.Clear()` clears the database and nulls the fields of [StaticReferences] classes. It knows nothing about caches the GAME keeps on its own types. And the game keeps one:
class HairStyleDec : Dec { public static readonly List<HairStyleDec> AllMaleStyles = new(); public static readonly List<HairStyleDec> AllFemaleStyles = new(); public override void PostLoad(...) { ... AllMaleStyles.Add(this); ... } // ← APPENDS }
Every `ParserModular.Finish()` runs `PostLoad` on every dec, so every parse APPENDS a whole fresh generation of HairStyleDecs on top of the last one — while only the FINAL generation is registered in the database. New pawns pick their hair from that LIST, not from the database:
HairStyle = (Gender == Female ? AllFemaleStyles : AllMaleStyles).PickRandomElement()
…so a pawn can be handed an instance the save writer will refuse: `WriteDec` compares by REFERENCE against the database and, on a mismatch, writes "<name>_DELETED" — which reads back as a silent NULL and NREs in `RigController.UpdateAppearance` during `Map.Activate`. The map never activates. The save is dead.
We parse more than once whenever a mod fails def validation (the bisect path in ). MEASURED: with one bad mod present, 6 parses → the lists held 6 copies of every style → 6 of 7 pawns were unsaveable. With no bad mod: 1 parse, 0 duplicates, every pawn saved cleanly.
── WHY BASELINE-RESTORE AND NOT JUST Clear() ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Clearing is only CORRECT for caches that `PostLoad` REPOPULATES. Reflection cannot distinguish those from a cache populated ONCE (a static initializer or a lazy snapshot of the database — the game already has one of those shape: `PlantDec[] AllCrops = Database<PlantDec>.List.Where(x => x.IsCrop)`). Blanket-clearing such a cache would empty it with nothing to refill it — a quieter, worse bug than the one we are fixing, shipped by the very code meant to prevent it.
So: snapshot each cache's PRISTINE contents once, before our first parse, and RESTORE to that baseline before each subsequent one. • append-on-PostLoad cache → baseline is empty → restore == clear → PostLoad refills it. ✔ • populated-once cache → baseline holds its contents → preserved. ✔ • a parse that THROWS → the caches are still restorable, not left empty. ✔ The right behaviour falls out of the baseline; we never have to guess which kind a cache is.

member.summary:
Decides whether a mod's Decs can be parsed against the game that is actually installed — before they are handed to the game's parser.
── WHY THIS EXISTS SEPARATELY FROM ────────────────────────────────────────── That one guards a mod's ASSEMBLY. This guards its CONTENT, and they fail independently: a mod with no code at all can still ship <ThingDec> against a build where the class is now EntityDec.
The legacy Dec.Parser takeover got this for free by dry-running each mod in isolation and dropping the ones that failed. That is not available on the modular path: Dec.Database is static, so a trial parse pollutes the very world the game is about to build — which is exactly the multi-generation dec corruption DecCacheGuard exists to prevent, and it is what made saves unloadable before. Validating by parsing means parsing twice, and parsing twice is the bug.
So this reads the XML instead. Every element directly under the document root names a dec CLASS, and every class="…" attribute names one too; both are resolved the way Dec itself resolves them — through Config.UsingNamespaces, read live rather than hardcoded, so the list cannot drift from the game's.
★ What this does NOT catch, said plainly: malformed XML, a renamed FIELD inside a dec, a missing parent, a bad enum value. It catches the dominant failure after a game update — a dec class that moved or vanished — and it cannot itself corrupt anything, because it parses text and touches no global state. A cheap check that is always safe to run beats a thorough one nobody dares enable.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.ModCompatibility
member.summary:
Decides whether a mod assembly can run against the game that is actually installed — BEFORE it is loaded.
── WHY THIS HAS TO HAPPEN FIRST ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── A mod compiled against an older build references game types by name. When the game renames them (build 24493575 moved the entire entity layer: Ascent.Things → Ascent.Entities, Thing → Entity), those references dangle. That is not a contained, mod-shaped failure:
Dec.Serialization.Initialize() enumerates the types of EVERY loaded assembly. One unresolvable mod assembly makes it throw, which throws out of the ParserModular CONSTRUCTOR, which fails GameRoot.LoadDecs() — and the base game comes up with ZERO content. Not "mods are broken": the GAME is broken, by a mod the player may not even remember installing.
Once the assembly is in the game's AssemblyLoadContext there is no taking it back — that context is not collectible, and it cannot be, because mod types must share identity with the game's. So the check must happen before the load, which means reading the file rather than loading it.
── HOW ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── System.Reflection.Metadata reads the assembly's TypeRef table straight off disk (in-box since .NET Core 3; no new dependency, and nothing is loaded). Every TypeRef scoped to the game assembly is looked up in the live game assembly. Anything missing is a reference that WILL dangle at runtime.
★ Deliberately checks only types scoped to the GAME assembly. Any other unresolved reference is either a framework issue or the mod's own business, and refusing to load a mod over a reference we do not understand would make this a source of false quarantines — which is how a safety check ends up disabled.

member.summary:
Manifest dependency resolution — MANIFEST-DEPS-001. Turns the discovered mod set plus each mod's declared constraints into a load order, and names every mod it had to exclude.
── WHY THIS EXISTS ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Load order was a hand-assigned integer in mod.json. That is fine while every mod is first-party and one person picks the numbers. It fails the moment two third-party authors both pick 100, or a mod calls into another mod's assembly that is not installed — which surfaces as a TypeLoadException from inside somebody else's code, with nothing naming the mod that actually needed it.
── THE INVARIANTS ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ★★ NEVER SILENT. Every mod that does not load appears in with a rule and a sentence naming the other mod. A resolver that quietly drops a mod is worse than no resolver: the player sees missing content and has nothing to search for.
★★ NEVER THROWS. Malformed input (a self-dependency, a cycle, a version string that is not a version) resolves to an exclusion, never an exception. This runs during boot, before the fault chokepoint has anything to catch for, so it must be total.
★★ DETERMINISTIC. Same mod set in, same order out, on every machine and every launch. All tie-breaks fall through to (LoadOrder, then id ordinal-ignore-case) — never to dictionary or directory order. Non-determinism here would make save compatibility and bug reports meaningless.
★ DECLARED EDGES OUTRANK THE INTEGER. If A requires B, A loads after B even if A's LoadOrder is lower. The integer only breaks ties between mods with no declared relationship, which preserves every existing manifest's behaviour (no edges declared ⇒ pure LoadOrder sort, exactly as today).
★ OPTIONAL IS THE DEFAULT POSTURE for anything the broker already makes safe. See .
── NOT WIRED YET ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Nothing in the live load path calls this. It is scaffolding: types, rules and tests, so the shape is settled and testable before ModLoaderCore depends on it. Wiring it is a separate, deliberate change (see HANDOFF_DEPENDENCIES.md §"Wiring", which also covers why declarations must move inside the signature envelope before this can gate anything for security rather than for correctness).

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.ModDiagnostics
member.summary:
The machine-readable account of what actually happened this boot — for every mod, and for the base game.
── WHY, WHEN THERE IS ALREADY A LOG ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── The log is a narrative: excellent for a human reading top to bottom, useless for a test. Asserting on it means grepping prose, and prose gets reworded. Worse, the interesting facts are scattered across it — a mod's signature verdict, whether its Init threw, whether the circuit breaker later disabled it, and what it cost per tick are four different lines in four different places, and NONE of them appears if the mod was rejected early.
So every mod is accounted for HERE, whatever its fate — loaded, disabled, rejected, or faulted — and the counts must reconcile: discovered == loaded + disabled + rejected. A mod that silently vanishes between discovery and loading is exactly the bug this makes impossible to miss.
── VANILLA ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── The loader sits inside the game with a view nothing outside it has: it can read Dec.Database.Count after the parse and say how much CONTENT the game actually loaded. That number is the base game's own integrity check — a game update that silently drops defs shows up as a count that moved, long before anybody notices a missing item in play. A log line cannot be diffed across builds; a number can.
★ Never throws, never gates loading. Diagnostics that can break the boot they describe are worthless.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.ModSaveData
member.summary:
Mod save-data attachment — a standard way for a mod to attach its own blob to the game's save and get it back on load, with a version for migration. The persistence dependency every *stateful* mod needs (the World Map's node state is its first consumer); built before that mod, not before all mods.
DESIGN — sidecar, not injection. AoA saves are a single dec-Recorder XML document written by the game. AshForge does NOT splice mod data into that document (that would couple every mod to dec's format and risk corrupting the base save). Instead each save file user://saves/<name>.xml gets a parallel sidecar <name>.xml.ashforge holding all mods' blobs. The sidecar is independent: it can't break the game save, it survives game updates, and a missing/corrupt sidecar just means mods load with no prior state.
── ⛔ ORPHANED SIDECARS, AND WHY WE DO NOT DELETE THEM ──────────────────────────────────────────────── The game deletes a save with File.Delete(fullName) on the .xml alone and its picker lists only *.xml, so our file is left behind. Two ways to handle that, and we deliberately take the second: 1. ✗ **Hook DeleteSave** — cannot work as written. DeleteSave opens a confirmation dialog and deletes inside the callback, so a postfix runs when the dialog is SHOWN: it would fire when the player cancels and not when they confirm. 2. ✗ **Sweep the saves folder** for sidecars with no matching save — works, and deletes a player's data on a guess. A save absent for a moment (cloud sync, a restore in progress, an external tool) would cost them their mod state permanently. Tidying is not worth that. 3. ✓ **Let them lie there, and make them INERT** — the origin check in refuses a sidecar from a different world, so an orphan can no longer do harm. It is a few KB of JSON. ★ The check also covers what no delete-hook could: a save COPIED, RENAMED, or restored from a backup outside the game. ⇒ correctness is enforced where the data is read, not by trying to police the filesystem.
LIFECYCLE (driven by ): save → (postfix SaveMenu.StartSaveToFile) load → (postfix SaveMenu.StartLoadFromFile — read sidecar off disk) → (postfix World.ActivateMap — hand each mod its blob exactly when the loaded world goes live, so a handler may touch World.Active)
Every provider callback runs through (THE INVARIANT) — a mod that throws while saving or loading is isolated and attributed, and never breaks the save, the load, or another mod's data.

Everything a mod ships that is NOT Assemblies/ or Decs/: textures, meshes, locale tables, incident definitions. Absent from a manifest ⇒ nothing extra to check, which is how every already-signed mod keeps verifying unchanged.
★★ WHY THIS IS A SECOND SET AND NOT A WIDER . The original rule was an ALLOWLIST — Assemblies/ and Decs/ were covered, everything else was continued, so an added file was not merely unsigned but not even NOTICED. That fails OPEN: every content directory invented after the rule was written landed outside it in silence. By 2026-07 four had, all inside mods that verified green — AshWorldMap's globe.glb/planet*.png/*.json (200 MB across 139 files), AshChains' Poses/ and Textures/, AshWealth's locale/ru.tsv (attacker-authored strings rendered to the player under a trusted badge), and AshEvents' Definitions/, which drives spawn / injure / despawn / publish from XML.
★★ AND WHY IT IS NOT SIMPLY INVERTED TO A DENYLIST. "Cover everything not explicitly mutable" sounds strictly better and is not, because it makes the mere APPEARANCE of a file fatal. A Thumbs.db beside WorldMap's root PNGs, a desktop.ini, a sync client's dropping — each becomes "unsigned code/content file" on a mod the player installed legitimately. Since 1.0.20 the signature gate has a player-facing toggle, so every false tamper alarm is an argument for switching verification OFF ecosystem-wide. A rule that fails closed per mod would fail open for everyone.
So the two questions are separated, because they have different answers: • TAMPERING — a listed file whose bytes changed. Checked for EVERYTHING, driven from the manifest. Cheap, and OS junk can never trigger it because junk is not listed. • ADDITION — an unlisted file appearing. Fatal only under enumerated_dirs, the directories the mod loads by WILDCARD (Assemblies/, Decs/, Definitions/), where a new file is executed or parsed rather than ignored. A stray file next to a texture is inert; a stray .xml in Definitions/ is an incident that fires.
★ The transition costs nothing. An old loader reads only key_id and files and ignores unknown fields — but the signature covers the RAW manifest bytes, so these fields are authenticated even on a loader that cannot read them. Leaving files as the legacy set therefore means a re-signed mod still verifies on every loader already in the field, and there is no flag day.

member.summary:
Per-mod isolation, all via reflection against dec (no compile-time dep).
1. — replaces dec's default error handlers (which RETHROW, so one bad def crashes the whole load) with non-throwing, logging versions. Backstop: no mod can hard- crash the def load.
2. — load base + every mod in ONE real parse and keep it if clean (no throwaway pre-parse — see the method for why a discarded parse corrupts saves). Only when that load errors does it bisect individual mods; bad mods are DISABLED + reported.
3. — the loader does the REAL load itself: base game + every good mod, each as its own ParserModular.Module in load order (so mods can patch/override base defs). The Harmony prefix then SKIPS the game's own Finish, avoiding the dec world-state corruption that happens if the game's parser finishes after our dry-runs cleared the database.
We use ParserModular directly (not the Parser wrapper we patched), so none of this re-enters our Harmony patch.

member.name: M:AshForge.ModLoader.ModValidator.ValidateAndLoad(System.Reflection.Assembly,System.String,System.Collections.Generic.List{AshForge.ModLoader.ModInfo})
member.summary:
Resolve the good mod set AND leave the live database loaded with exactly it, doing a SINGLE full parse on the happy path.
Why single-parse matters: every full parse runs the game's dec PostLoad side effects, and some of those populate game-side caches with dec instances. If we parse once to *validate* and then throw that away and parse again to *load*, a game cache can be left holding instances from the discarded parse while the live database owns different ones — and dec serialises a reference whose object ≠ the database's as <name>_DELETED, so a game saved that session won't re-load (it crashes restoring the missing dec). So: attempt the REAL combined load (base + every mod) and, if it's clean, keep it — no throwaway pre-parse, no stale instances. Only if the combined load actually errors do we bisect individual mods (which re-parses); that path is rare (a genuinely broken mod) and self-heals next launch once the validation cache makes the load a single clean parse.

member.name: M:AshForge.ModLoader.ModValidator.BisectAndResolve(System.Reflection.Assembly,System.String,System.Collections.Generic.List{AshForge.ModLoader.ModInfo})
member.summary:
Find the broken mods (the error path, only when the combined load failed), then resolve any conflicts among the survivors.
★★ GROUP TESTING, NOT ONE-AT-A-TIME. This used to dry-run every mod individually — O(N) FULL dec parses, each re-parsing the entire base game (540 decs), each ~1.1-1.5 s even at 3 mods and slower as the mod count climbs. One bad mod among 500 meant ~500 parses: a load screen measured in TENS OF MINUTES.
A parse tells us "does this SET contain a problem", so we can ask about a whole GROUP at once and halve: if a group parses clean, every mod in it is exonerated in ONE parse. One bad mod in 500 now costs ~9 parses instead of 500, and k bad mods cost about k·log(N/k).
★ A group can also fail because two mods in it CONFLICT while each is fine alone. Then both halves come back clean, we correctly blame nobody, and picks it up — which is exactly where that case belongs.

Its paths come from ProjectSettings.GlobalizePath and it logs through GD.Print — both Godot native calls, dead outside the engine process. A standalone harness could only ever measure a re-implementation, and a benchmark of a stand-in measures the stand-in.

One honest sample. • the CURVE comes from the same primitives it uses — Dec's Recorder over ModMetaData and over the order/active lists, plus the directory scan — driven with synthetic data in a temp folder that touches no game state at all.

member.summary:
Makes AshForge mods appear — and behave — in the game's own Mods dialog (build 24493575+).
── WHAT THE GAME'S MOD SYSTEM ACTUALLY DOES ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Ascent.Engine.ModManager scans <game>/Mods/<dir>/About.xml, keyed by DIRECTORY NAME, and remembers two lists in user://: ModOrder.xml (every mod it has ever seen) and ActiveMods.xml (the ticked ones). For an active mod it loads Assembly/*.dll and registers Dec/. There is no entry point of any kind — assemblies are loaded so Dec can resolve types against them, and nothing is ever called.
── WHY A STUB, NOT A MOVE ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── AshForge mods live outside the game install (under AshForgeModLoader/mods) and the game scans only <game>/Mods. So each mod gets a stub directory there containing About.xml and NOTHING ELSE — no Assembly/, no Dec/. The dialog lists it; the game loads nothing from it; AshLoader keeps loading the real mod from the real place. That absence is the entire reason there is no double-load, so it is load bearing: never "helpfully" populate a stub.
── WHY THE TICKBOX HAD TO BE HONOURED, NOT JUST SHOWN ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── The dialog derives each tickbox from activeMods.Contains(dir). Publishing stubs WITHOUT seeding ActiveMods would render every AshForge mod unticked while it was in fact running, and unticking one would do nothing — a UI that states the opposite of the truth and ignores the user. That is worse than no integration at all, so enable state is genuinely shared:

The game deletes a save with File.Delete(fullName) on the .xml alone and its picker lists only *.xml, so it neither knows nor cares that our file exists. Delete a colony, start a new one, and name it the same thing — the obvious thing a player does — and the orphaned sidecar is read back into a game that never had it: stale raid rosters, stale economy, a stale faction ledger. ★★ A DELETE HOOK ALONE CANNOT FIX THIS. It would stop orphans accumulating, but a save copied, renamed, or restored from a backup outside the game produces the same collision with no delete involved. Only something carried INSIDE the sidecar and checked against the loaded world closes it.
── WHY THE HOME MAP'S SEED ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── The save document carries no world id — World.Record writes its managers and its two map slots and nothing identifying. But every map records a MapData, and MapData.Seed is a ulong fixed when the world is generated and round-tripped forever after. The HOME map is the one map a colony always has and never swaps, so its seed is the colony's identity for as long as it exists.

If the probe cannot answer, the sidecar is honoured exactly as it is today — the pre-existing behaviour, bug and all. Refusing mod data because OUR probe broke would turn a rare collision into a guaranteed loss of everyone's mod state on the next game update.

member.summary:

Loader-drawn and mod-drawn are equally defeatable AFTER load. That is not the difference that matters. • The difference is BEFORE load. A mod-drawn indicator is removable with a checkbox — the same Mod Manager the player is already in. The attack is then one extra sentence of social engineering ("and turn off the AshForge status mod"), which needs no malware and leaves no trace. Drawing it in the loader forces an attacker into active tamper, which is unambiguous malice and leaves evidence.
So the rule is narrowed rather than discarded: a mod draws FEATURES; the loader draws the one control whose whole value is that the thing it warns about cannot switch it off.

Four test projects consume AshLoader through a ProjectReference, and the mod csprojs show the Linux build resolves the game via $(GameData); a hardcoded GodotSharp HintPath here would flow into all of them and break the Linux loader build. This is also just the loader's existing idiom: it never compile-references dec or the game assembly either. The ENTIRE Godot surface is the handful of lookups in — one place to fix when Godot moves, one canary to fail. Verified against GodotSharp 4.3.0.0.
